story.name: ジャスミンの きっさてん
story.title: Opening Day, in the Rain
story.line: あめの なか、オープンの ひです
story.ja: オープンの日はどしゃぶり。最初の1時間、だれも来ない。ジャスミンが泣きそうになったとき、レインコートのちゃちゃまるが来る。それからキャラメル、きぬよ、たぬきちも。店はぬれた傘でいっぱいになり、牛乳がなくなって、ちゃちゃまるが雨の中を家まで取りに走る。ドアの前には、Bとだけ書かれたコーヒー豆の袋が置いてあった。

segments.en: Sunday morning, it rained. Not a little rain. It was the kind of rain that bounces off the pier and comes down sideways, like it's in a hurry.
Pekoe had been up since five. The cups were lined up. The honey toast was ready to go into the oven. The machine was warm and humming.
At eight o'clock exactly, she turned the little sign on the door from closed to open, and she stood behind the counter, and she waited.
Nobody came. The rain drummed on the roof. The clock ticked. Every now and then, a seagull walked past the window, looked inside, and kept walking.
It's fine. It's totally fine. It's early, it's raining. Nobody wants to go out in this. It's fine.
By nine, it didn't feel fine. She sat down on a stool and looked at the five things on her little menu, and her eyes started to sting.
And then the door banged open, and a big yellow raincoat came in, dripping all over the clean floor. Inside the raincoat was Dom.
Sorry I'm late! I did my run first. Bad idea. Really bad idea. Can I get the biggest coffee you've got?
Pekoe made him the biggest coffee she had ever made. Her hands were shaking a little.
He drank it at the counter and said it was the best coffee on the island.
Ten minutes later, Goldie came in under a polka-dot umbrella, with a book under her arm. She sat by the window and ordered a pot of black tea.
I'm planning to stay a while, if that's okay. Rainy days are reading days. This is my spot now, by the way.
Then Mabel came, to check that the curtains looked right in the rain. They did.
She ordered a latte and stayed to fix one cushion that didn't need fixing.
Then Tom Nook arrived with his two nephews, who each had a hot cocoa and argued about who had more marshmallows. They had exactly the same number.
What a lovely place you've made, Pekoe. Yes, yes. And look at all these people. On a day like this, too!
By ten thirty, every seat was full.
There was a row of wet umbrellas by the door, the windows were fogged up, and the whole café smelled like coffee and toast.
People who had never really talked to each other were sharing tables. Somebody was laughing in the corner. It was loud and warm, and it was exactly right.
And then, in the middle of all that, Pekoe opened the fridge and saw that she was almost out of milk.
Oh no. No, no, no. I'm running out of milk. I've got, like, two lattes left. Maybe one and a half.
Say no more. I'm on it. I've got a fridge full of milk at home, for my shakes. Back in five. Maybe four, if I sprint.
And before she could say anything, the yellow raincoat was gone, out into the rain.
He was back in six minutes, completely soaked, holding four bottles of milk over his head.
Everybody in the café clapped. Dom took a bow, slipped on the wet floor, and sat down very suddenly. Then everybody clapped again.
Around noon, Pekoe went to put the umbrellas in a neater row, and she found something by the door that she hadn't noticed before.
It was a heavy paper bag of coffee beans, the good kind, dark and shiny. There was a note tied to it with string, in very neat handwriting.
It said, good luck today. Remember, be patient. And under that, just one letter. B.
Who's B? Wait, is that from Brewster? Oh my gosh, that's so sweet. Is he coming in today?
He didn't come that day. But Pekoe put the note up on the wall, right next to the napkin with his advice on it.
When the last customer left, the rain had finally stopped.
Pekoe sat at the counter in the empty café, surrounded by cups, and she smiled until her face hurt.

predict.ask: マスターは いつ 来る？
choices: He comes on the next rainy day with an umbrella for everyone.
A few weeks later, on his day off, he finally comes in as a customer.
predict.ja: 数週間後、休みの日に、ついに客として来る。
